abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

abstract: Conventional and transgenic approaches to crop improvement are increasingly constrained by biosafety concerns, stringent regulatory frameworks, and limited public acceptance, necessitating new precision breeding methods. DNA-free genome editing using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach has emerged as a transformative approach that enables precise, targeted genetic modifications without the stable integration of a foreign gene (transgene). This strategy transiently introduces CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, or in vitro transcribed mRNA, into plant cells. This review focuses primarily on CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing and its applications in crop improvement. After targeted genome cleavage, the editing elements are rapidly degraded, leaving only the desired genomic modification and resulting in plants indistinguishable from those developed through conventional breeding. To achieve targeted, DNA-free genome editing, researchers have developed numerous molecular platforms and delivery systems, such as protoplast transfection, biolistic bombardment, nanoparticle-based systems, and emerging pollen- and meristem-targeted systems, for major crop species. Researchers have successfully enhanced several notable traits, including disease and pest resistance, nutritional quality, abiotic stress tolerance, and agronomic performance, in cereals, vegetables, oilseeds, and perennial crops. Recent advancements, including base editing, prime editing, and multiplex gene editing, are further expanding the precision, efficiency, and scope of DNA-free genome editing. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing offers a route to crop improvement that avoids stable transgene integration, though its wider deployment depends on progress in regeneration, molecular validation, and regulatory convergence.

title: A new capless self-amplifying RNA.

abstract: The growing resistance to antibiotics by Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a global health threat. Traditional antibiotics act on the viability of bacteria, whereas new ones are now increasingly targeting virulence factors. Phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) are essential virulence factors that play important roles in inflammation, neutrophil lysis, cytotoxicity and biofilm formation. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were used for literature search of articles published between 2010 and 2026. Green-synthesized metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been found to be capable of altering these mechanisms by inducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, membrane damage, and by interfering with the quorum-sensing mechanism of the bacteria, along with inhibiting the Agr system. Optimization of NP-based interventions can be supported by multi-omics approaches such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Other potential methods of targeted PSM pathway and Agr pathway suppression are also available, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and dCas9, but there are delivery difficulties. The potential use of combining nanotechnology, gene editing, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology could allow for development of more advanced anti-virulence strategies against S. aureus infections targeted at PSM.

title: Targeting phenol-soluble modulins: eco-friendly theragnostic strategies against Staphylococcus aureus biofilms.

abstract: Salvia miltiorrhiza Bunge is a valuable medicinal plant, yet its genetic manipulation has been limited by the lack of efficient and practical transformation methods. Here, we report a simplified, tissue culture-independent strategy enabling Agrobacterium-mediated gene delivery under non-sterile conditions, termed hypocotyl acupuncture. The method employs needle-assisted inoculation of intact seedlings at the hypocotyl, completely bypassing callus induction, regeneration, and repeated subculture. Following inoculation, EGFP-positive hairy roots are selectively cultivated for approximately 4 months and then induced to regenerate shoots within one additional month, yielding transgenic plantlets in approximately 5 months. Systematic optimization achieved a transformation efficiency of approximately 55% (defined as the percentage of explants producing EGFP-positive regenerants). ACCC10060 was selected as the optimal strain based on efficiency and root morphology. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing generated mutation frequencies of 53.8%-88.9% with no off-target effects. Targeted mutagenesis of SmCPS1, a gene encoding a key rate-limiting enzyme in tanshinone biosynthesis, resulted in altered root pigmentation. The method was successfully extended to Astragalus membranaceus, Platycodon grandiflorus, and Isatis indigotica, achieving transformation efficiencies of 25%-55%. This study provides an efficient, practical, and broadly applicable tool for genome editing and functional genomics in medicinal plants.

title: Hypocotyl acupuncture: an efficient and practical protocol for transformation and genome editing in Salvia miltiorrhiza.

abstract: Land plant mitochondria and plastids are endosymbiotic organelles that possess their own, reduced genomes. Gene expression is largely regulated at the transcript level, predominantly by nuclear-encoded proteins. Notably, up to thousands of cytidines in organellar RNAs are specifically edited to uridines, mostly restoring conserved genetic information. Key players in this process are nuclear-encoded pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, which bind target RNAs in a one-PPR:one-nucleotide manner, following a two-amino-acid-based code. Cytidine deamination is catalyzed by intrinsic or trans-acting DYW domains. The modularity and programmability of PPR-RNA interactions make PPR editing factors attractive candidates for the development of biotechnological tools. However, RNA target selection is not determined by the 'PPR code' alone, hampering the generation of highly effective and specific editors. Refining such tools requires efficient assays to dissect the determinants of editor-RNA interaction. Here, we introduce a rapid assay to assess PPR editor specificity through transient expression in the cytosol of Nicotiana benthamiana, which offers a large and diverse transcriptome that enables extensive off-target editing. Profiling of these off-targets provides comprehensive information on an editor's target selectivity. Compared with a previous setup in the model moss Physcomitrium patens, which relies on stable transformation, the required experimental time is reduced from months to days. We demonstrate the power of the system by characterizing the off-targets of the moss editor PpPPR56. The new assay allows rapid functional assessment of editing factor variants and removes a bottleneck in understanding editor-RNA interactions, which is a prerequisite for the rational improvement of PPR-based RNA editing tools.

title: A rapid and efficient in planta assay for assessment of RNA editing factor performance.

abstract: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) remains one of the most important staple crops worldwide and serves as a primary source of calories and protein for billions of people. Global wheat production, however, continues to be threatened by rust diseases caused by Puccinia triticina, Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici and Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. These pathogens are highly adaptive and frequently give rise to new virulent races, causing resistance in wheat cultivars to breakdown. Under favorable environmental conditions, severe epidemics can develop and substantial yield losses may occur. In response to these challenges, traditional management approaches such as resistant cultivars, crop rotation, sanitation and fungicide application have long been employed in wheat production systems. Yet these strategies have increasingly been constrained by resistance breakdown, genetic uniformity in modern cultivars, and climate-driven changes in pathogen distribution. Conventional management practices are evaluated alongside emerging technological solutions including genomic-assisted breeding, gene pyramiding, CRISPR-based genome editing, biological control agents and precision agriculture tools. In addition, nanotechnology has emerged as a promising tool in plant disease management, where nanoparticles such as silver, copper and zinc oxide exhibit strong antifungal activity and enable targeted delivery of agrochemicals. Nano-enabled formulations can enhance fungicide efficiency, reduce chemical inputs and improve plant defense responses, offering a sustainable complement to existing wheat rust management strategies. Particular attention is given to integrated disease management strategies, which combine traditional agronomic practices with modern surveillance technologies such as remote sensing, artificial intelligence-based forecasting models, and pathogen genomics. These combined approaches can improve resistance durability and build more resilient wheat production systems. Future directions emphasize climate adaptation, global surveillance and collaborative breeding. In an era of increasing climatic uncertainty and evolving pathogen populations, durable rust management will depend on coordinated global efforts that align scientific innovation, farmer adoption, and policy support to safeguard wheat productivity and global food security.

title: Wheat Rust Diseases: Global Impact, Integrated Disease Management, and Emerging Biotechnological Innovations for Sustainable Crop Protection.

abstract: Dendrobium officinale is an important medicinal Orchidaceae species with considerable ecological and economic value. While its chloroplast genome has been well characterized, the structure features of its mitochondrial genome remain largely unexplored, which further hinders our understanding of its evolutionary dynamics and adaptive mechanisms. This study presents a comprehensive characterization of the mitochondrial genome of D. officinale, revealing a complex multibranched structure of 22 chromosomes totaling 639,931 bp, encoding 35 PCGs, 3 rRNA genes, and 24 tRNA genes. Codon usage analysis revealed a distinct codon bias, while the genome harbors abundant repetitive elements and 522 RNA editing sites. Comparative genomic analysis identified 125 MTPT fragments totaling 108,012 bp (16.88% of the mitogenome), indicating frequent inter-organellar DNA transfer. Dendrobium nobile exhibited the highest genomic homology with D. officinale. Ka/Ks analysis indicated that most mitochondrial genes are under strong purifying selection. In addition, we conducted a comparative analysis between the newly assembled mitochondrial genome of D. officinale and seven Orchidaceae species. Phylogenetic analysis based on the maximum likelihood, maximum parsimony and bayesian inference approaches resolved the phylogenetic position of D. officinale within Orchidaceae. Collectively, these findings provide a valuable reference for future studies on Orchidaceae phylogenomics and mitochondrial evolution.

abstract: Understanding how an RNA recognizes small molecule ligands is crucial for pharmaceutical research. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can potentially reveal this process in atomistic detail. However, simulations frequently fail should energy barriers along the pathway prove to be insurmountably high on the simulation timescale (ns-µs). To address this limitation, we present a novel strategy combining well-tempered metadynamics utilizing X-ray crystallography or NMR-solved hydrogen-bonding interactions between an RNA and its ligand as collective variables (CVs). This approach can sample multiple transitions during the binding process and determine the most favorable binding modes through the reconstructed free energy landscape. Our computational recovery of binding modes for all five cases studied is in good agreement (RMSD below 2.0 Å) with the experimentally determined structures of the bound complexes. Our study demonstrates that metadynamics coupled with strategically chosen collective variables can effectively sample binding pathways and recover binding modes for RNA-small molecule complexes. This method therefore could be valuable for crystal structure interpretation, NMR solution structure refinement, and computer-aided design of RNA-targeted small molecule drugs.

abstract: Genome editing is becoming an important tool for crop improvement by enabling precise modification of genetic variation. CRISPR-Cas technologies have expanded beyond nuclease-induced mutations to include base and prime editing, transcriptional and epigenetic regulation, multiplex editing, organelle editing and targeted DNA insertion. These advances support the development of agronomically valuable alleles and extend crop improvement beyond conventional selection, recombination and random mutagenesis. Applications now include plant architecture, yield-related traits, resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses, seed composition and nutritional quality, and extend to de novo domestication, haploid induction and hybrid breeding. Current research is increasingly moving from single-gene modification toward the engineering of promoters, cis-regulatory elements, quantitative alleles and multiple-gene editing, particularly in polyploid crops. Wider breeding applications will depend on efficient delivery and regeneration, recovery of transgene-free and heritable edited germplasm, reliable targeted insertion and validation across relevant environments. Integration with pangenomics, multi-omics, phenomics, artificial intelligence and predictive breeding may further improve target identification, allele design and prediction of editing outcomes, thereby supporting the development of more precise and efficient crop-breeding strategies.

abstract: In June 2026, satri-cel/CT041, a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell product targeting Claudin18.2, received approval from China's National Medical Products Administration for the treatment of Claudin18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma after failure of at least two prior lines of therapy. This marks the first CAR-T product approved worldwide for solid tumours. The approval ends the long-standing debate over whether CAR-T cells can be effective against solid malignancies, yet it simultaneously raises a more pointed issue: in its pivotal randomised controlled trial, median progression-free survival was 3.25 months (95% CI 2.86-4.53) with satri-cel against 1.77 months (95% CI 1.61-2.04) with treatment of physician's choice, giving a hazard ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.24-0.56). The two medians differ by 1.48 months; that figure marks where each survival distribution is cut in half and is not the benefit any individual patient can expect, and approval does not equate to a cure. Taking this as a starting point, this review systematically dissects the immunological bottlenecks that constrain CAR-T efficacy in gastrointestinal tumours. We first trace the evidence chain from phase I studies through the randomised controlled trial to exploratory adjuvant-therapy settings and then integrate the landscape of targets-Claudin18.2, glypican-3, carcinoembryonic antigen, mesothelin, and CDH17-within a target-tumour matrix encompassing gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic cancer. The core section focuses on four intertwined immunological constraints: spatiotemporal heterogeneity and escape at the antigen level; a therapeutic window shaped jointly by epitope masking within tight junctions and immune privilege of the gastric mucosal stem cell niche-this mechanism not only explains why Claudin18.2-directed CAR-T cells exhibit an acceptable safety profile despite target expression on normal tissues but also provides a paradigm for rational selection of next-generation targets; a suppressive microenvironment composed of regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, tumour-associated macrophages, transforming growth factor-β, adenosine, and a hypoxic and acidotic metabolic milieu; and CAR-T exhaustion driven by chronic antigen stimulation. We particularly emphasise that metabolic stress and exhaustion are not two parallel obstacles. We put forward a mechanistic model in which persistent antigen stimulation combined with intratumoral hypoxia acts as a "double hit": through mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species accumulation, the two inputs raise nuclear factor of activated T-cell (NFAT) activity and so drive the TOX/NR4A-dominated exhaustion program. This model is assembled from chronic-infection and mouse tumour systems and has not been tested in human CAR-T cells or in satri-cel-treated patients. We advance it as a framework for organising the four bottlenecks and for explaining why single-point interventions struggle to lift the efficacy ceiling, not as a demonstrated account. On this basis, we discuss strategies such as armouring, logic gating, transcription factor engineering, gene editing, and chemokine receptor modification, along with combination regimens involving checkpoint inhibition, oncolytic viruses, locoregional administration, and microbiome modulation, and we evaluate alternative platforms including CAR-macrophages, CAR-NK cells, and in vivo CAR-T generation. The watershed has been crossed, but the work of turning 3 months into 30 has only just begun.

abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is one of the most prevalent degenerative joint diseases, and there is no approved pharmacological therapy that can reliably reverse cartilage degeneration or restore cartilage structure. Allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have shown therapeutic potential for OA, but inflammatory conditions can enhance HLA expression and increase allogeneic immune recognition risk. Here, we generated B2M and CIITA double-knockout induced pluripotent stem cells (dKO-iPSCs) using CRISPR/Cas9 and subsequently differentiated them into dKO-iMSCs. B2M/CIITA double-knockout did not affect iPSC pluripotency, karyotype, or teratoma formation. dKO-iMSCs retained characteristic MSC phenotypes, exhibited greater proliferative capacity than tissue-derived MSCs, and could be expanded to passage 18. Notably, HLA-ABC and HLA-DR expression remained undetectable in dKO-iMSCs even after IFN-γ stimulation. In co-culture assays with PHA-L-stimulated allogeneic PBMCs, dKO-iMSCs suppressed PBMC and T-cell proliferation as effectively as wild-type iMSCs, indicating preservation of their immunomodulatory activity. Intra-articular administration of dKO-iMSCs significantly reduced cartilage degeneration in the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse model of OA. The treatment showed greater therapeutic efficacy than wild-type iMSCs and tissue-derived MSCs and did not cause evident systemic organ toxicity. Single-cell RNA sequencing of BM-MSCs and dKO-iMSCs after in vitro IFN-γ stimulation revealed enhanced extracellular matrix-associated cell-cell communication and markedly reduced IL1B expression in dKO-iMSCs, indicating a less pro-inflammatory and more matrix-supportive cellular state under inflammatory conditions. Collectively, B2M/CIITA double-knockout enables sustained reduction in HLA expression while preserving the MSC phenotype and immunomodulatory activity, and enhances the therapeutic efficacy of iMSCs in the mouse OA model, providing a potential strategy for developing iPSC-derived MSCs with reduced HLA expression for allogeneic cell therapy.

abstract: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere maintenance mechanism that supports the growth of approximately 5-10% of human tumors and represents an attractive but insufficiently explored therapeutic target. CRISPR-based functional genomics has emerged as a powerful approach to systematically interrogate ALT biology and identify genetic dependencies associated with the ALT state. In this Review, we discuss the CRISPR-based strategies applied to ALT, including hypothesis-driven targeted loss-of-function screens, phenotype-driven optical screens, in silico mining of large-scale dependency datasets, and genome-wide screens in ALT-adjacent states. Across these approaches, recurrent dependencies converge on pathways mediating replication stress buffering, DNA repair, and telomere maintenance, including FANCM, SMARCAL1, and SUB1. Collectively, these findings support a model in which ALT-positive cells rely not on a unique ALT-specific factor, but rather on stress-buffering mechanisms that prevent chronic telomeric dysfunction from triggering replication catastrophe and cell death, highlighting these pathways as promising candidates for further therapeutic investigation.

abstract: Single-stranded DNA breaks (SSBs) at repetitive elements promote internal loops (i-loops), precursors of extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA). Here, we present a protocol for inducing targeted breaks at human telomeric or alpha-satellite repeats using doxycycline-inducible Cas9 nickase variants and repeat-specific sgRNAs. We describe steps for verifying strand-specific nicking by alkaline-gel Southern blotting and detecting i-loop accumulation by two-dimensional agarose gel electrophoresis (2D gel). In this protocol, DNase I treatment of isolated nuclei is employed as a Cas9-independent control. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Zanella et al.1.

abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) poses a significant global health challenge, lacking FDA-approved pharmacotherapies. Despite extensive exploration of therapeutic targets and interventions, effective treatment remains scarce due to challenges in delivering therapeutic agents to relevant brain regions at effective concentrations. Nanoparticle-mediated delivery offers a promising approach for transporting various therapeutic cargos to the central nervous system, including small molecules, nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and gene-editing systems. However, the application of nanomedicine strategies in addressing the unique pathophysiological characteristics of MUD has not been systematically assessed. This review presents a problem-focused analysis of how lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, biological, and hybrid nanocarriers tackle successive delivery obstacles such as systemic stability, blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, brain region-specific distribution, and controlled release of intracellular cargo. We compare preclinical nanotherapeutic approaches encompassing small-molecule neuroprotective agents, anti-METH vaccines, gene-silencing RNAs, neurotrophic proteins, and emerging gene-editing methods, outlining their respective benefits, limitations, and design considerations. Additionally, we explore key factors influencing nanomedicine performance in MUD, including protein corona formation, the impact of METH-related BBB dysfunction and neuroinflammation on nanoparticle distribution, and the disparity between acute animal models and chronic human MUD with relapse tendencies. In conclusion, we present a systematic framework for aligning nanocarrier characteristics with distinct delivery obstacles and therapeutic needs. We also emphasize forthcoming avenues such as disease-triggered nanocarriers, targeted delivery to specific regions, combined nanomedical approaches, theranostic strategies, and standardized assessments of biodistribution, effectiveness, safety, and translational potential.

abstract: Ex vivo expansion is a fundamental yet challenging step in the manufacturing of adoptive cell therapies (ACT), as therapeutic success relies on generating enough functional immune cells while maintaining their phenotype, metabolic fitness, and persistence. This review provides a comprehensive overview of immunomodulatory strategies designed to enhance cell yield during ex vivo expansion, categorizing them into cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic approaches. Cell-intrinsic strategies, including gene editing and gene transfer technologies, enable precise modulation of survival pathways, proliferation, metabolic state, and resistance to exhaustion. These tools support the production of more potent and durable immune cell products. In contrast, cell-extrinsic strategies shape immune cell behavior through cytokine supplementation, checkpoint blockade, nutrient and metabolic modulation, feeder cell systems, synthetic activation platforms, and biophysical cues such as oxygen tension and bioreactor-controlled environments. Together, these strategies provide coordinated signals that direct activation, differentiation, and persistence during expansion in culture. The review also highlights key regulatory considerations, including distinctions between genetically and non-genetically modified products, risk assessments associated with human and animal-derived materials, ancillary material qualification, and process scalability for clinical translation. By integrating biological, engineering, and regulatory perspectives, this paper outlines principles for scalable immunomodulation platforms designed with regulatory considerations in mind to advance next-generation ACT manufacturing.

abstract: RNA-based genetic cargos have emerged as versatile tools in both fundamental research and translational medicine, with growing applications in regenerative medicine, gene therapy, cell therapy, and vaccination. As the field advances beyond single-RNA delivery, coordinated engineering of multiple RNA species is enabling increasingly sophisticated and combinatorial biological functions. However, this shift raises a fundamental challenge: what combination and stoichiometry of RNA species should be delivered together to achieve a desired cellular function? As the number of RNA components increases, the design space expands combinatorially, making conventional optimization strategies labor-intensive and poorly scalable. Here, we introduce StoichRNA, a framework for scalable exploration of multi-RNA stoichiometry in a single experiment. Individual RNA species are delivered independently, each coupled to a distinct fluorescent marker that reports its intracellular abundance. Because uptake is stochastic, each cell acquires a unique combination and copy number of RNA components. Across a sufficiently large population, cells collectively sample a broad stoichiometric landscape, allowing single-cell readouts such as flow cytometry to quantitatively map system output as a function of intracellular RNA composition. We first establish the conceptual validity of this approach by showing that StoichRNA-derived single-cell data can recover and predict the behavior of fixed-ratio RNA formulations. We then apply this framework to representative RNA circuits, demonstrating that StoichRNA can reveal design principles and identify improved stoichiometries that would be difficult to uncover through conventional workflows. Finally, we extend StoichRNA optimization to translationally relevant settings, including control of cell-state engineering in human induced pluripotent stem cells and tuning of RNA-based logic circuits for precision medicine applications. Together, these results establish StoichRNA as a generalizable strategy for engineering combinatorial RNA systems and provide a scalable solution to a central bottleneck in RNA circuit design.

abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of updated strain-containing compositions of the mRNA-1010 vaccines within the current epidemiological environment.
description:
This study uses a master protocol with a generic study design to allow flexibility in evaluating immunogenicity and safety of updated strain-containing compositions of the mRNA-1010 vaccines. As different strain-containing vaccine compositions will be evaluated, each study intervention will be described in the subprotocol. For each evaluation of an updated strain, a new subprotocol will be generated. Reported outcome measures are based upon each subprotocol. Not all reported outcome measures may be applicable to each subprotocol.

Subprotocol 01 is to evaluate the 2026-2027 mRNA influenza vaccine.

abstract: Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation is a central process that shapes immune responses across diverse contexts, yet how inflammatory cues engage metabolism to instruct monocyte fate commitment remains unclear. Here, using a CRISPR-based metabolic screen combined with monocyte-specific perturbations in bacterial lung infection, we identified lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) as a key metabolic regulator of monocyte commitment to the nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2)+ macrophage fate in vivo. LDHA-dependent cytosolic nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) regeneration enabled selective hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1α) translation through its 5' untranslated region (UTR) and is associated with structural remodeling of this region. HIF1α then functioned as a downstream effector that promoted the NOS2+ macrophage fate. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) further acted as an upstream metabolic priming signal that enhanced LDHA-dependent HIF1α regulation and supported this differentiation process. Together, these findings suggest that metabolic redox state regulates monocyte fate commitment through selective mRNA translation coupled to RNA structural remodeling.

abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

abstract: Crustacean aquaculture, particularly shrimp, crab, and lobster production, contributes around US$10 billion annually to the global food supply but remains highly vulnerable to viral and bacterial diseases. Pathogens such as White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV), Yellow Head Virus (YHV), Taura Syndrome Virus (TSV), and Vibrio species continue to cause substantial economic losses, and conventional management based on visual inspection, histopathology, and antimicrobial treatment is often slow and insensitive. This review examines how nucleic acid technologies are reshaping diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance in crustacean health management. Molecular diagnostic platforms including PCR, quantitative PCR, reverse transcription PCR, loop mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, and multiplex assays allow rapid, sensitive, and specific detection of pathogens, often before clinical signs appear. RNA interference shows strong therapeutic promise against viral pathogens, with experimental studies reporting 40 to 80% reductions in cumulative mortality, although stability, dosing, delivery, and production cost continue to limit commercial use. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) and Cas (CRISPR-associated) has emerged as a powerful platform for functional genomics, immune gene characterisation, and the future development of disease resistant strains, though application in crustaceans remains largely proof of concept. Environmental DNA and molecular biosurveillance enable early pathogen detection through water and sediment sampling, supporting proactive biosecurity and precision aquaculture. Persistent barriers include scalability, infrastructure gaps in producing regions, regulatory uncertainty, and public acceptance. Future progress will rely on improved delivery systems, expanded crustacean genomic resources, and integration of molecular tools with digital farm management to deliver sustainable disease control.

abstract: One of the major contributors to persistent healthcare and community-associated infections is S. aureus, which has a remarkable ability to form biofilms that protect it against the host immune system and antimicrobial therapy. In recent years, it has become clear that biofilm development is a highly orchestrated and dynamic process, controlled by complex genetic networks, transcriptional regulators, two-component systems (TCSs), and environmental signals. The present review covers the molecular mechanisms involved in the initiation, maturation, maintenance, and dispersal of biofilms in general, and in particular, the coordinated functions of adhesins, the icaADBC operon, components of the extracellular matrix (ECM), global regulators (agr, sarA, and sigB), and two-component regulatory systems, as well as emerging insights from transcriptomic studies on biofilm adaptation. We then review the roles of these regulatory pathways in metabolic heterogeneity, antibiotic tolerance, immune evasion, and persistence in clinically relevant biofilm-associated infections, including infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, catheter-associated infection, and diabetic foot infection. The review further outlines the latest developments in antibiofilm therapeutics, including matrix-degrading enzymes, quorum-sensing inhibitors, antimicrobial peptides, bacteriophage-based therapeutics, lysins, nitric oxide donors, nanoparticle-assisted therapeutics, and CRISPR-Cas-based antimicrobials. Incorporating molecular regulation into infection-specific pathogenesis and emerging therapeutic strategies, this review offers a new perspective on the biology of S. aureus biofilms and highlights opportunities to develop mechanism-based interventions to combat chronic biofilm-associated infections.

abstract: Plant mitochondrial genomes are structurally dynamic and contribute to energy metabolism and stress responses. Comparative mitogenomic analyses of closely related species occupying contrasting elevations can provide insights into mitochondrial genomic differentiation across elevational environments. Using PacBio HiFi reads, we assembled and compared the mitochondrial genomes of the higher-altitude species R. alpina and the lower-altitude species R. purpurea. Both mitochondrial genome assemblies yielded graph-like structures, with R. alpina exhibiting a more complex assembly-graph topology, more dispersed repeats, and extensive evidence of dispersed-repeat-mediated recombination. Despite these structural differences, the two species retained broadly similar core gene complements, codon-usage patterns, and predicted RNA-editing profiles. Among genes represented by multiple annotated copies in both species, 12 had higher annotated copy numbers in R. alpina. Most shared protein-coding genes were highly conserved, whereas nad4 and rps3 each contained two nonsynonymous substitutions between the two species. Genes with higher annotated copy numbers and those showing limited sequence divergence were both annotated into respiratory complex I and mitochondrial translation. These results reveal pronounced differentiation in mitochondrial genome architecture alongside strong conservation of coding characteristics. Both the differences in gene representation and the limited sequence divergence converge on the same functional processes, suggesting a potential link between mitochondrial genomic changes and adaptation to high-altitude environments. We hypothesize that these genomic features may be relevant to the physiological performance of R. alpina in a high-altitude environment.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains the deadliest form of leukemia in children and adults despite therapeutic advances in recent decades. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy is one such therapeutic approach that has been explored preclinically and clinically in AML; however, its efficacy is limited by antigen heterogeneity. To overcome this roadblock, we propose a dual-targeting CAR T-cell strategy, targeting the AML-associated antigens CD33 and CD70.
METHODS: To recapitulate tumor heterogeneity, we genetically edited the AML cell line Molm-13 using CRISPR-Cas9 to generate distinct sublines, namely CD33+/CD70-, CD33-/CD70+, and CD33+/CD70+. Two dual-targeting CAR T-cell approaches were developed: a "pooled" product, in which CAR T cells directed towards CD33 or CD70 are combined and co-administered, and a "co-transduced" product, wherein one population of T cells is transduced with both CD33-CAR- and CD70-CAR-encoding viral vectors.
RESULTS: Pooled and co-transduced products demonstrated potent cytotoxicity against all Molm-13 populations, whereas single-antigen CAR approaches were not as effective when their respective target antigen was absent. Mice engrafted with CD33/CD70 heterogeneous Molm-13 cells were treated with pooled or co-transduced CD33/CD70 CAR T cells. Both groups exhibited a significant survival advantage over the untreated group, with the co-transduced approach showing a statistically significant advantage over the pooled group.
CONCLUSIONS: In summary, engineering one T cell to express both CARs yielded superior cytotoxicity when targeting a heterogeneous AML blast population.

abstract: In this edition, we highlight several important developments across the Huntington's disease therapeutic pipeline. We discuss the launch and subsequent discontinuation of POINT-HD, the first-in-human phase I study of RG6496 (Hoffmann-La Roche), an allele-selective antisense oligonucleotide designed to selectively lower mutant huntingtin while largely preserving wild-type huntingtin expression. We also discuss the launch of two phase III efficacy trials: INVEST-HD, evaluating votoplam (Novartis Pharmaceuticals), and PRECISE-HD, evaluating pridopidine (Prilenia). In addition, we summarise recent advances across the field, including preclinical updates for LQT-23 (LoQus23), SRP-1005 (Sarepta Therapeutics) and HRN001 (Harness Therapeutics); interim 12-month clinical results from SKY-0515 (Skyhawk Therapeutics); the announcement by uniQure that 3-year data from the phase I/II AMT-130 study may support a Biologics License Application seeking accelerated approval and Roche's discontinuation of the phase II GENERATION HD2 study of tominersen. Finally, we provide an updated listing of registered and ongoing clinical trials in Huntington's disease.

abstract: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.

title: The advances and challenges of mRNA-LNP application in fields of hematology and oncology therapeutics.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed RNA therapeutics through their high delivery efficiency, scalable manufacturing, and favorable safety profiles, as demonstrated by COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and clinically approved small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutics. However, extending RNA delivery beyond the liver to extrahepatic tissues, including the spleen, lungs, lymph nodes, brain, and tumors, remains challenging because of the intrinsic hepatotropism of conventional LNPs and their limited cell-type specificity. Recent advances in lipid chemistry, particle engineering, surface functionalization, protein corona modulation, and route-specific administration have enabled new strategies to redirect LNPs toward specific tissues and cell populations. This review systematically examines these approaches and highlights key determinants of LNP tropism, including formulation composition, surface properties, endogenous protein adsorption, and administration route. We further discuss the clinical translation of extrahepatic LNP delivery, covering clinically validated products, emerging therapeutic candidates, and gaps between preclinical models and human applications. Major challenges include cell-resolved biodistribution, long-term safety, repeated-dose immunogenicity, cross-study comparability, and standardized quantitative assessment. Finally, we explore how high-throughput screening, machine learning, and data-driven design can accelerate the rational optimization of next-generation LNPs. These advances may facilitate precise tissue- and cell-selective RNA delivery, expanding the therapeutic potential of RNA medicines beyond the liver.

abstract: Introduction In February 2025, a single infant with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency received a customized base-editing therapy, and individualized gene editing has since been discussed as an emerging category of care. No one has yet counted whether this category exists in the registered study record. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional census of interventional studies of human gene-editing agents registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. Records were retrieved through the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface, version 2, with a verbatim, intervention-scoped query and a fixed census date of 17 September 2026. Eligibility was verified from each record's own fields, and every exclusion is supported by the field value that justifies it. Two independent screening passes classified each eligible record as single-participant or n-of-1, multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated, or conventional cohort. Agreement was quantified with Cohen's kappa and a 95% confidence interval (CI). Records in the individualized and platform classes were re-verified against their complete registry entries and version histories. We also searched public US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) records for the regulatory route of each census record. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. Results Of 212 retrieved records, 64 were excluded, and 148 were eligible. Four eligible records were single-participant or n-of-1 designs, and three were multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated designs, giving a census of seven studies. Of the remainder, 140 were conventional cohorts, and one was an editing arm inside a non-editing platform trial. Version histories confirmed the four single-participant designs; one of them reached an enrolment of one through a revision made before enrolment began. The same histories showed that three other records had an enrolment of one or two only because of termination or under-enrolment. Only two of the 148 eligible records describe a construct designed for the individual participant. No publicly verifiable platform technology designation was located for any census record, and the census query returned no expanded-access record. Of 23 studies completed more than 12 months before the census, five had posted results (21.7%, Wilson 95% CI: 9.7%-41.9%); because this interval is wide, the figure is reported as context only. Agreement on design class was moderate (kappa, 0.540; 95% CI, 0.264-0.815). Conclusions Nineteen months after the first individualized CRISPR treatment, the registry contains seven individualized or platform-designated gene-editing studies, and only two records describe an individualized construct. The regulatory pathway used by the index case was not retrievable from the registry, and no regulatory route could be verified from public records; this is an absence of public evidence, not evidence that no route existed. These counts describe the ClinicalTrials.gov record, not the prevalence of individualized gene editing, and the design-class counts are provisional given moderate agreement.

title: Individualized and Platform-Designated Gene-Editing Studies in the Registered Clinical Record: A Case-by-Case Census Against 148 Eligible Studies.

abstract: Infant neuroblastoma (NB), defined by diagnosis during the first year of life, represents a clinically heterogeneous disease spectrum ranging from localized tumours with favourable outcomes and a capacity for spontaneous regression, to high-risk metastatic disease requiring intensive multimodal therapy. In infants, treatment intensity is determined by disease stage, tumor biology, MYCN status, risk classification, symptoms, response to therapy, and metastatic involvement, particularly relevant to high-risk disease, consequently the potential toxicity of intensive treatment is specific to high-risk disease, as compared to favorable risk tumors which can be managed with surgery, reduced frequency techniques, or observations. Important determinations of neuroblastoma biology and prognosis are genetic alterations involving MYCN and ALK, but the predominately investigated field with therapeutic feasibility of targeting these changes with CRISPR/Cas9 is in preclinical neuroblastoma models rather than in infants. An investigational hypothesis is accordingly considered by their potential relevance to infant neuroblastoma rather than an established clinical application. The safe and efficient in vivo delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 components remains a major challenge, owing to cargo size, immunogenicity, and degradation, particularly within the delicate physiological environment of infants. This review emphasises the need for advanced delivery systems, focusing on the potential of nanoparticle-mediated approaches. Emerging preclinical findings support the feasibility of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 delivery, although direct evidence in infant neuroblastoma remains limited. Importantly, the evidence for nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 therapy remains largely preclinical. Studies performed in general neuroblastoma models, non-cancer models, or adult cancers should not be interpreted as direct evidence of efficacy in infant neuroblastoma.

title: Precision gene editing in infant neuroblastoma: a review of nanoparticle: enabled CRISPR/Cas9 therapies.

abstract: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers have emerged as powerful molecular tools for cancer imaging, biosensing, and biomarker detection due to their high specificity, low background fluorescence, and genetic encodability. These short RNA molecules activate fluorescence upon binding specific fluorogens, enabling real-time visualization of intracellular targets and dynamic molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances in RNA structural engineering, fluorophore optimization, and biosensor integration have significantly expanded the translational applications of fluorogenic aptamers in oncology. This mini-review summarizes the structural principles, fluorescence activation mechanisms, and cancer-related applications of fluorogenic RNA aptamers and related nucleic acid biosensors. Foundational studies describing the architecture of fluorogenic aptamer families, including Spinach, Broccoli, Mango, Pepper, Squash, and Beetroot, are discussed with emphasis on G-quadruplex-mediated fluorogen stabilization and fluorescence enhancement. Furthermore, recent developments in CRISPR/Cas-assisted fluorogenic biosensors, dual-color RNA imaging systems, fluorogenic DNAzymes, and amplification-driven aptamer platforms are highlighted. Direct applications across multiple malignancies, including brain, breast, colorectal, liver, lung, prostate, and skin cancers, demonstrate the growing utility of these technologies for tumor-associated RNA detection, epigenetic biomarker analysis, molecular imaging, and therapeutic monitoring. In addition, advances in fluorescence brightness, structural stability, and multiplex imaging strategies have improved the sensitivity and adaptability of fluorogenic RNA systems for complex biological environments. Despite current limitations related to RNA stability, intracellular delivery, and tissue penetration, fluorogenic RNA aptamers represent highly promising tools for next-generation precision oncology. Continued integration with nanotechnology, live-cell imaging, artificial intelligence, and molecular diagnostics is expected to enhance further their clinical and translational potential in cancer research and personalized medicine.

abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

abstract:
MOTIVATION: Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations.
RESULTS: We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79,648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing.
AVAILABILITY: CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a pivotal regulator of cholesterol homeostasis, primarily known for inducing the degradation of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). Beyond this classical pathway, PCSK9 exerts complex pleiotropic effects and interacts with various lipoproteins, contributing to cardiovascular and metabolic pathologies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on PCSK9 biology, its multi-organ implications and evolving therapeutic strategies.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes current evidence from experimental, translational and clinical studies on PCSK9 biology and therapeutics. The literature examined includes studies on PCSK9 transcriptional regulation, post-translational modifications, interactions with lipoproteins and the clinical development of established and emerging PCSK9-targeting therapies.
RESULTS: PCSK9 activity is modulated by several transcription factors (e.g., SREBP2, HNF1α) and post-translational processes such as furin cleavage and sulfation. Clinically, elevated PCSK9 levels are linked to atherosclerosis progression, heart failure and adverse outcomes in infectious diseases and certain malignancies. Monoclonal antibodies (alirocumab, evolocumab) and siRNA (inclisiran) consistently reduce LDL-C by 50%-60%. Emerging approaches include oral inhibitors which may broaden access to PCSK9-targeting therapy, and CRISPR-based gene-editing strategies (e.g., VERVE-102), which aim to achieve sustained LDL-C lowering after a single treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: PCSK9 is a multifaceted protein with roles extending far beyond LDL-C regulation. Understanding its diverse interactions is crucial for optimizing treatment in cardiovascular disease and potentially expanding its therapeutic application to metabolic and infectious conditions.

title: Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9: From Biology to Therapeutic Targeting in Cardiovascular Disease.

abstract:
AIMS: Selenoprotein T (SELENOT) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident thioredoxin-like oxidoreductase implicated in redox and calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis and protein quality control. Although SELENOT is highly expressed in the brain, its role in hypothalamic pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons, which regulate energy balance, remains poorly understood. We investigated whether SELENOT is required for maintaining ER homeostasis and neuronal integrity in POMC neurons.
RESULTS: Using CRISPR-edited and siRNA-silenced POMC neuronal models together with a POMC-specific SELENOT knockout mouse, we demonstrated that SELENOT loss induces a senescent-like phenotype including cellular hypertrophy, loss of neurite outgrowth, senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity, increased P16 and P21 expression, and acquisition of senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Senescence markers were elevated not only in SELENOT-deficient POMC neurons but also throughout the surrounding arcuate nucleus in vivo, suggesting propagation of a pro-inflammatory microenvironment. Mechanistically, prolonged SELENOT deficiency produced selective activation of the ATF6α arm of the unfolded protein response, depletion of ER Ca2+ stores, and profound alterations in N-glycan maturation. Notably, leptin-induced POMC processing and secretion were spared. Glycomics revealed a shift toward immature glycans, whereas thiol-trapping proteomics identified candidate SELENOT interactors linked to ER Ca2+ regulation.
INNOVATION AND CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first evidence that SELENOT deficiency is sufficient to trigger cellular senescence in POMC neurons, acting as a central regulator integrating ER proteostasis, Ca2+ homeostasis, redox adaptation, and glycosylation. These results reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism potentially linking neuronal senescence to hypothalamic dysfunction and suggest that SELENOT-dependent pathways may represent therapeutic targets for obesity, metabolic disease, and age-related neuroendocrine disorders. abstract: Nanomedicine has become an important translational platform in oncology by enabling altered pharmacokinetics, controlled exposure, reduced systemic toxicity, intracellular delivery of nucleic acids, and improved handling of complex therapeutic payloads. Early cancer nanomedicines, including pegylated liposomal cytotoxics and albumin-bound drug products, demonstrated that nanoscale formulation design could improve the clinical utility of established anticancer agents. More recently, lipid nanoparticles, RNA therapeutics, individualized neoantigen vaccines, gene-regulatory approaches, and immune-modulating delivery systems have expanded the role of nanoparticles from passive drug carriers to programmable oncology platforms. This narrative review examines the developmental evolution of cancer-focused pharmaceutical nanoparticles, with emphasis on liposomes, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), albumin-bound systems, polymeric particles, polymeric micelles, nanocrystals, nanoemulsions, solid lipid nanoparticles, inorganic particles, extracellular vesicles, and hybrid delivery technologies. Each platform class is treated systematically, covering representative approved products, formulation characteristics, route of administration, clinical evidence, and the specific development risks that limit it. There view connects platform design with oncology-specific barriers, including tumor heterogeneity, variable enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effects, dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, mononuclear phagocyte clearance, protein-corona formation, endosomal escape, immune activation, and the difficulty of translating animal tumor models into clinical benefit. These barriers are organized as a sequential delivery cascade, and the behavior of each platform class is compared step by step rather than described as a set of universal phenomena. Nanoparticle candidates that accumulated well in preclinical tumors but failed in clinical trials are examined alongside approved products, because the contrast between the two is where most of the transferable lessons sit. A product-development perspective is used to discuss critical quality attributes (CQAs), manufacturing scalability, potency testing, sterility strategy, stability, release methods, regulatory expectations, commercial feasibility, and clinical differentiation. A development-to-translation framework is proposed for comparing cancer nanomedicine platforms across formulation maturity, analytical maturity, manufacturing maturity, biological rationale, clinical evidence, regulatory readiness, and commercial feasibility; regulatory and commercial maturity are scored separately, the criteria behind each level are defined explicitly, and the resulting rankings are presented as a heuristic aid to discussion rather than a validated quantitative metric. Future progress in oncology nanomedicine will depend not only on novel materials or targeting claims, but also on disciplined product design, biologically meaningful potency assays, scalable manufacturing, patient-selection strategies, and clear integration with precision oncology.

abstract: This is an open-label, dose escalation study in patients with relapsed and refractory autoimmune diseases. Study drug, TI-0032-III injection, is composed of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) targeting T cells that encapsulate circular RNA encoding the CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), which is a therapeutic biological product. It is clinically intended for the treatment of various relapsed and refractory B cell-related autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sjögren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, and antiphospholipid syndrome.

abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) poses a serious global health threat, undermining treatment outcomes and necessitating the development of innovative therapeutic strategies. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major contributor to this burden, with increasing prevalence in hospitals, contaminated food, and environmental sources. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further intensified S. aureus resistance due to widespread antibiotic misuse. Biofilm formation, which facilitates the horizontal transfer of resistance genes such as mecA (methicillin resistance gene A), plays a central role in the development of resistance. To counteract antibiotic-resistant S. aureus, alternative approaches have emerged, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), photodynamic therapy (PDT), and drug repurposing guided by artificial intelligence (AI). Cutting-edge technologies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based gene editing and engineered bacteriophages offer promising avenues for targeting resistant strains. Natural compounds such as thymol and chlorogenic acid (CGA) have also shown potential in reducing resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. Effective management of AMR requires strengthened antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs), robust surveillance systems, and public health measures such as proper hand hygiene and environmental sanitation. Combining antibiotic adjuvants (AAs) with existing antibiotics and leveraging bioactive peptides (BAPs) can enhance antibiotic efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-drug-resistant (PDR) S. aureus. This review investigates the prevalence and resistance mechanisms of S. aureus in clinical, food, and environmental contexts, explores promising alternative therapies, and emphasizes the urgent need for global antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) and sustainable intervention strategies.

abstract: Obesity leads to metabolic dysregulation and thus drives complications including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, steatotic liver disease and some cancers. Obesity is primarily driven by lifestyle factors, which impacts individuals differently depending on their genetic susceptibility. Studies on this genetic risk have provided major insights into gene networks that modulate obesity development, including incretins and their regulatory circuits. Indeed, incretin-based therapeutics (i.e. GLP1 RA) have proven to be enormously successful in promoting weight loss, but do so with several ongoing challenges including significant weight rebound upon cessation, loss of lean mass, and side effects that reduce therapeutic longevity. Thus, ongoing research is necessary to identify additional interventions that overcome or minimise these concerns. To this end, in our previous work we have identified a novel lipid regulatory protein with potential to influence lipid storage. In the current study, we use antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) to silence this protein in mouse models of diet induced obesity, and demonstrate that once weekly IP injections of ASO prevents the development of obesity, and defends against the progression of existing obesity. This is shown to be effective in multiple mouse strains fed different diets over various time frames, with gene targeting ASOs leading to reductions in fat mass, no change in lean mass, along with improvements in whole body glucose tolerance and steatotic liver disease. Additional studies demonstrate that this phenotype is likely driven by effects in adipose tissue, but not liver, and is not linked to activation of the Type 1 Interferon response, a previously implicated off target effect of ASO administration. Thus, these studies demonstrate that our injectable ASO approach in mice can successfully treat obesity in the absence of major change in lean mass, thus positioning this intervention as a therapeutic program that works alternatively to, or in conjunction with current weight loss medicines.

abstract: Trypanosoma brucei and Leishmania tarentolae are model kinetoplastids whose mitochondria contain a unique DNA network, kinetoplast DNA (kDNA), and exhibit specialized features, including developmental remodeling and RNA editing. By integrating mass spectrometry-based protein correlation profiling with published datasets, we assembled inventories of 1,666 mitochondrial proteins in T. brucei and 1,594 in L. tarentolae. These include 124 polypeptides not previously recognized as mitochondrial. Despite their phylogenetic distance, trypanosomes and leishmanias maintain highly conserved mitoproteomes, including about 700 components with no detectable homologs in other eukaryotes. Comparison of T. brucei insect and mammalian stages revealed similar mitoproteome compositions but globally reduced mitochondrial protein abundance in the latter, except for components of calcium homeostasis and the alternative oxidase pathway. We also detected ten kDNA-encoded proteins, including products of pan-edited transcripts. These inventories establish a framework for functional analysis of previously uncharacterized mitochondrial factors and illuminate innovations that have shaped kinetoplastid evolution.

abstract: The Microprocessor complex, minimally composed of DROSHA and DGCR8, is ubiquitously required for microRNA biogenesis. It also regulates the balance between pluripotency and differentiation through mRNA alternative splicing and mRNA cleavage. However, how these various activities are regulated remains incompletely understood. Both DROSHA and DGCR8 are phosphoproteins, and phosphorylation has been reported to influence their molecular functions. In this study, we identified residues in DGCR8 by mass spectrometry that were differentially phosphorylated in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) before and after differentiation into neuronal cells. This included S95 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in undifferentiated cells, and S238 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in differentiated cells. By means of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing of the endogenous Dgcr8 gene, we generated a homozygous S95A mESC clone and a heterozygous S238A/- mESC clone. Both mutants retained an mESC phenotype but exhibited altered Microprocessor-dependent functions and differentiation outcomes. When directed toward the neuronal lineage, the S238A/- mutant displayed elevated mRNA expression of neuronal progenitor markers even after 10 days, while both S95A and S238A/- mutants failed to generate cardiomyocytes in embryoid body differentiation cultures. Furthermore, MEK1/2 inhibition with a highly selective inhibitor partially phenocopied the transcriptional effects of S95A in mESCs, consistent with a potential contribution of ERK/MAPK signaling for S95 phosphorylation. Together, these findings support a role for site-specific DGCR8 phosphorylation in modulating Microprocessor-dependent processes and differentiation in mESCs, establishing DGCR8 phosphorylation as an important regulatory mechanism in the regulation of Microprocessor activity, especially for stem cell differentiation.

abstract: This is a Phase 1b/2 open-label study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and clinical effects of intravenous (IV) WVE-N531 in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). To participate in the study, patients must have a documented mutation of the DMD gene that is amenable to exon 53 skipping intervention. This study has 3 parts, Part A, Part B, including Part B Extension Arm, and Part C. Part A is completed. Part B is completed. Following completion of Part B, all patients elected to continue to receive study drug in the optional Part B open-label Extension Arm. Part C has been added to the study and will enroll new patients.
description:
Following completion of Part A, eligible patients rolled over into Part B to continue to receive treatment. In addition, new patients were enrolled up to a total of 11 patients in Part B. All patients received WVE-N531 at 10 mg/kg every other week (Q2W) until competent authority approval of a protocol update, when all patients were switched to Q4W dosing. Muscle biopsies were performed following 24 weeks and for new Part B patients (those that did not take part in Part A) following 48 weeks of treatment. Following completion of Part B, all patients elected to continue to receive study drug at Q4W for up to 1 year in an optional Part B Extension Arm.

In part C of the study, 13 new patients have been enrolled . All patients will undergo an open muscle biopsy, at baseline and following 24 weeks of treatment.

The primary endpoint for Part B is the measurement of dystrophin protein levels. Participants will also be evaluated for safety, tolerability, digital and functional endpoints.

The primary endpoint for Part C is the measurement of dystrophin protein levels. Participants will also be evaluated for safety, tolerability, digital and functional endpoints. Safety monitoring will occur through 10 months after the last dose.

abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold immense therapeutic potential, yet their clinical translation is hindered by nonspecific cellular uptake and the complexity and cost of surface engineering. Here, we present the EZON (Easy OligoNucleotide) EV modification platform, a cost-effective, post-isolation modification system that addresses both limitations simultaneously. The EZON platform employs unmodified DNA aptamers that bind directly to tetraspanin proteins on EV surfaces, eliminating the need for cholesterol conjugation, covalent chemistry, or genetic engineering of producer cells. EVs are thus easily and rapidly functionalized in a single incubation step at substantially reduced oligonucleotide cost. The EZON platform enables dual functionality: (1) the oligonucleotide anchor (ONA) sequence inhibits nonspecific cellular uptake, while (2) the display strand enables targeted delivery through ligand-mediated internalization. We demonstrate that our optimized ONA construct efficiently functionalizes EVs from multiple mammalian cell types. Cancer cells selectively internalized EZON-modified EVs functionalized with AS1411, an aptamer that targets nucleolin, whereas off-target internalization was suppressed. The platform's versatility extends to protein display via histidine-tag aptamers and therapeutic cargo delivery, as demonstrated by targeted doxorubicin delivery to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells. This rapid, modular approach transforms unmodified EVs into precision delivery vehicles within hours, offering a scalable solution for targeted therapeutics.

abstract: Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) have emerged as an effective experimental platform for bridging the long-standing gap between traditional in vitro cancer models and the biological complexity of actual tumors. These three-dimensional cultures (3D), derived directly from patient tissues, preserve essential architectural, genomic, and phenotypic characteristics of their tumors of origin, enabling more accurate modeling of tumor heterogeneity and disease evolution. Over the last decade, rapid methodological advances in organoid culture systems, extracellular matrices (ECMs), and growth factor optimization have facilitated the establishment of organoid models for a wide range of malignancies and the development of large living biobanks representing diverse patient populations. These models are increasingly being utilized to study cancer biology, elucidate mechanisms of treatment resistance, and evaluate patient-specific therapeutic responses, highlighting their potential as tools for precision oncology. However, important challenges remain, including incomplete representation of the tumor microenvironment (TME), variability in culture conditions, and limited scalability, and the need for greater standardization and validation. Consequently, although PDOs show considerable promise for translational research and personalized medicine, their routine clinical implementation remains largely investigational, and their clinical utility has not yet been fully established. This review examines the technological foundations of PDO generation, assesses their role as experimental models of tumor biology, and discusses their expanding applications in translational cancer research and precision oncology while highlighting key challenges that must be addressed before their widespread clinical adoption.

abstract: Mitochondria, as organelles with a critical role in maintaining cellular activities, are also vulnerable to dysfunction, which contributes substantially to the pathogenesis of various systemic diseases. Nanomaterials, owing to their tunable physicochemical properties and precise bio-interfacial capabilities, offer innovative platforms not only for delivering general mitochondria-targeted therapy but also for enabling-with promising potential-the emerging paradigms of mitochondrial transfer and transplantation. Nevertheless, a dedicated review systematically summarizing progress in this specific subfield is lacking. To fill this knowledge gap, this review provides a structured synthesis that spans from the biological basis of mitochondrial function and transfer to the broad applications of nanomaterials in mitochondria-targeted therapies, with a dedicated analysis of their roles in mitochondrial targeting, functional modulation, and gene editing. A key topic of this review is the emerging role of nanomaterials in assisting mitochondrial transplantation and transfer. By integrating these insights, this work bridges nanotechnology and mitochondrial medicine, offering a valuable resource for developing organelle-specific therapeutics.

abstract: Apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), and ApoE4-directed gene editing and gene therapy have emerged as promising therapeutic strategies for AD, although they remain investigational and are not yet an established mainstream treatment. Interestingly, however, ApoE4 is reported to be associated with a reduced risk of retinal degenerative diseases such as glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and diabetic retinopathy (DR). Therefore, should ApoE4 gene editing therapy be approached with caution when AD occurs concurrently with glaucoma, AMD, or DR? In view of these and based on the existing literature, the present study detailed the distinct roles of ApoE4 in AD, glaucoma, AMD, and DR, with a purpose to offer valuable insights into subsequent ApoE4 gene editing therapies. We also summarise the ApoE-targeted therapeutic programmes currently in preclinical and early clinical development, delineate the remaining translational challenges, and discuss how patients with coexisting retinal neurodegenerative disease might be evaluated and monitored.
