abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have reshaped modern vaccinology by enabling rapid antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and coordinated induction of humoral and cellular immunity. Their clinical success has established mRNA as a versatile platform for infectious diseases, cancer immunotherapy, and emerging therapeutic applications. However, expansion into cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, autoimmune, and metabolic disorders imposes indication-specific requirements that cannot be addressed by uniform design strategies. Vaccine performance depends not only on antigen output, but also on how RNA architecture and delivery systems regulate innate sensing, intracellular trafficking, tissue distribution, and adaptive immune programming. In this review, we summarize bioengineering strategies for improving mRNA vaccine immunogenicity by coordinating antigen-expression efficiency with innate immune regulation. We compare non-replicating mRNA, self-amplifying RNA, and circular RNA in terms of expression kinetics, translational logic, safety considerations, and innate immune activation. We then discuss molecular engineering approaches that enhance stability, translation, and immune control, including optimization of cap structures, untranslated regions, poly(A) tails, nucleotide modifications, codon usage, and platform-specific designs for saRNA and circRNA. We further examine delivery systems, including lipid nanoparticles, exosomes, polymer-based carriers, virus-like particles, and hybrid platforms, emphasizing their dual roles in cargo transport and immune modulation. Finally, we discuss indication-specific design principles, manufacturing constraints, and translational challenges. We propose that next-generation mRNA vaccines will require disease-matched co-design of RNA molecules and delivery platforms to enhance antigen expression, tune immune activation, and strengthen clinical translation.

abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification

abstract: Reliable assessment of disease status and therapeutic response in osteosarcoma remains an unmet clinical need. Integrative bioinformatics analysis and protein-level verification in paired clinical specimens prioritized secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1, osteopontin) as a liquid biopsy target associated with osteosarcoma progression and patient survival. On this basis, CRUMP, a CRISPR-Cas12a and FUSE Probe-based dual-mode biosensing platform, was developed for SPP1 quantification. A bifunctional NH2-ZIF-8 probe co-immobilizes the components required for target recognition and Cas12a activation, while MoS2@AuNPs interfaces transduce the resulting signals. Signal amplification is achieved through a unipoint-anchored multisite cascade based on a DNA tetrahedron-HCR architecture, enabling one-to-multiple parallel amplification while balancing stability and sensitivity. A single Cas12a cleavage event simultaneously decreases the electrochemical (EC) signal and increases the fluorescence (FL) signal. These reciprocal changes allow the two readouts to provide an internal consistency check for each measurement. Each channel covers more than five orders of magnitude, with detection limits of 167.7 fg/mL for EC and 331.6 fg/mL for FL. The broad measurement ranges allow most serum samples to be analyzed directly, without the per-sample dilution optimization that ELISA requires, and the complete analysis takes only approximately 85 min. Validation across osteosarcoma cell lines, clinical specimens, and tumor-bearing mouse models provided preliminary evidence for the feasibility of CRUMP in SPP1 quantification and endpoint assessment of chemotherapeutic response. By combining biomarker prioritization, biosensor engineering, and preliminary application testing, this work presents CRUMP as a candidate platform for SPP1-based assessment of osteosarcoma and its therapeutic response.

title: Unipoint-anchored cascade amplification strategy integrating FUSE probe-activated CRISPR-Cas12a for dual mode osteopontin detection toward osteosarcoma assessment and therapeutic response evaluation.

abstract: Degenerative diseases continue to impose a substantial global health burden with limited curative options. Neurodegenerative diseases, the principal focus of this review, are among the largest contributors to this burden. Stem cell therapies have emerged as a promising approach, offering the potential to replace lost cells, modulate pathological microenvironments, and restore tissue function through both direct cell replacement and paracrine mechanisms. However, conventional stem cell strategies encounter persistent obstacles including immune rejection, tumorigenicity, poor engraftment, and limited long-term efficacy in chronic disease settings. This narrative review synthesizes recent and emerging innovations in stem cell therapy for neurodegenerative diseases across four major domains: (i) emerging mechanisms of stem cell action, including activation of dormant neural stem cells (NSCs), exosome-based cell-free therapies, and rejuvenation of aged stem cells; (ii) emerging cell types such as pre-morula stem cells (PMSCs), perinatal stem cells, SSEA-4+ human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUC-MSCs), and iPSC-derived mesenchymal progenitor cells (MiMPCs); (iii) advanced delivery platforms including three-dimensional (3D) biomaterial scaffolds, injectable hydrogels, and stem cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CMNPs); and (iv) gene-editing strategies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9-mediated generation of hypoimmunogenic induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines for allogeneic, off-the-shelf cell therapies. Key translational gaps, including standardization of exosome isolation and scaffold fabrication protocols, long-term safety and immunogenicity assessment, and ethical and regulatory frameworks, are critically evaluated, and future research directions are proposed. In addition, the review states the level of evidence (in vitro, animal, or human) supporting each approach and summarizes their clinical status in a single table. Addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to realizing the full potential of stem cell-based regenerative medicine for degenerative diseases.

abstract: Reactive oxygen species generate a family of oxidized guanine species that serve as important biomarkers of oxidative damage. Here, we report the development of a fluorogenic RNA switch that selectively recognizes oxidized guanine species. We first systematically characterized an oxidized guanine RNA aptamer, defining its minimum functional binding domain and molecular recognition profile. Structural minimization produced a compact aptamer with higher affinity than the full-length sequence that retained broad recognition of structurally diverse oxidized guanine species while discriminating against their unmodified counterparts. We subsequently incorporated the optimized aptamer into fluorogenic RNA switch architectures, revealing that fluorescence activation required iterative optimization of aptamer topology, scaffold architecture, and communication-linker design. The resulting fluorogenic RNA switch exhibited target-dependent fluorescence activation while retaining the aptamer's molecular recognition profile. This work establishes a fluorogenic RNA switch for oxidized guanine species and highlights the importance of systematic aptamer characterization and optimization in fluorogenic RNA switch development.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens human, animal, agricultural, and environmental health, driven by horizontal and vertical gene transfer. Conventional wastewater treatment removes 63-94% of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) but fails to eliminate ARGs and antibiotic-resistant bacteria, while generating toxic sludge. This review evaluates advanced biomaterials, including silver and gold nanoparticles, reactive oxygen species, magnetic nanocomposites, targeted disruption of metabolic pathways, carbon-based sorbents, biopolymers, metal-organic frameworks, functionalized enzymes/peptides, and engineered biofilms, for reducing ARG and resistant-bacteria loads, inhibiting horizontal gene transfer, and reducing the selective pressure exerted by residual antibiotics. These approaches offer enhanced performance across wastewater/agriculture/air/food supply chain systems. Challenges in scalability, ecological safety, and regulation remain, requiring integration with AI monitoring, CRISPR tools, and One Health strategies. This review aims to summarize and discuss the literature on the development and use of innovative biomaterial-based intervention strategies that address the environmental aspects of AMR in order to provide a comprehensive overview of what has been learned and developed to date.

abstract: Epigenetic regulation and gene transcription are dynamically modulated by extracellular signals, including focal adhesions; however, the role of integrins in these processes remains poorly understood. In this study in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, (HNSCC), we combined investigations in physiological three-dimensional, matrix-embedded cell models and patient-derived organoids with multi-omics analyses, bioinformatics and artificial intelligence, to unmask the integrin effector signaling network that reshapes chromatin to drive cancer. Among the 12 α/β1 integrin receptors, α7 integrin (ITGA7) emerged as the most potent modulator of histone post-translational modifications, associated with significant changes in gene transcription and chromatin accessibility. Depletion of ITGA7, achieved independently by CRISPR/Cas9 knockout and RNA interference, reduced chromatin accessibility at the AURKA locus and downregulated an AURKA-centered transcriptional program. Mechanistically, phosphoproteomics revealed significant inhibition of MAPK- and PI3K/AKT-dependent signaling with concomitant functional impairment of cell cycling and cell survival upon ITGA7 depletion. Across all analyses, machine-learning-based feature selection consistently nominated AURKA as the dominant downstream node, and tumor ITGA7 expression stratified patient overall survival in a non-linear manner. In summary, these findings establish α7 integrin as a key co-regulator of chromatin accessibility and gene transcription in HPV-negative HNSCC, acting through an AURKA-centered axis that couples adhesion signaling to cell cycle control and patient survival, and nominate AURKA, potentially targetable with clinical Aurora-A inhibitors such as alisertib, as an actionable therapeutic node downstream of the currently non-druggable ITGA7.

abstract: Spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the primary auditory afferents in the inner ear, are vulnerable to degeneration from neuropathies, concussion, and aging, among other causes. Accurate quantification of SGNs is critical for assessing degeneration and therapeutic interventions, but manual counting is arduous due to dense cellular crowding and unreliable nuclear markers. Because SGNs receive input from GluA2-containing AMPA receptors, the transcripts for which must be RNA-edited for calcium impermeability, we hypothesized that SGNs express high levels of the RNA-editing enzyme ADARB1. Here, we confirm enriched expression of Adarb1 transcripts in SGNs and show that anti-ADARB1 antibodies robustly label the nuclei of type I and type II SGNs from young and aged mice, adult macaques, and adult humans. Neuronal versus glial specificity was confirmed using antibodies against neurofilament heavy chain (NFH), human antigen D (HuD), GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3), and SRY-box 2 (SOX2). A blinded investigator manually counted mouse SGNs via NFH, and these were compared to automated counts of ADARB1-positive nuclei using the analyze particles function in ImageJ. A concordance correlation coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated strong agreement between the manual and automated counts. Together, these results suggest broad utility of ADARB1 immunolabeling for automated counts of SGNs across species.

abstract: Sepsis-induced myocardial dysfunction (SIMD) and related myocardial fibrosis (MF) contribute to poor cardiovascular outcomes. Whether the role of Nppb in this process remains unknown. This study aimed to investigate the effect of Nppb on MF in SIMD. Myocardial-specific Nppb conditional knockout (CKO) mice were generated using CRISPR/Cas9, and 8-week-old male mice were divided into control, sepsis, CKO control, and CKO sepsis groups. Cardiac function, histopathology, myocardial injury markers, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT)-related gene expression, and Notch1 signaling were measured. Nppb CKO alleviated myocardial injury, improved left ventricular systolic function, attenuated myocardial structural damage, suppressed EndMT, and increased survival in septic mice. Myocardial expression of Notch1 and Notch Intracellular Domain (NICD) was reduced in the LPS group but restored by Nppb CKO. In conclusion, myocardial Nppb deficiency protects against SIMD by maintaining cardiac contractility and structural stability, with associated changes in the Notch1 signaling pathway. Inhibiting Nppb may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for sepsis-related myocardial injury.

abstract: The "metal ion hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained widespread acceptance, but translating this understanding into effective therapies remains elusive. This likely stems from a simplistic understanding of metal homeostasis as merely a matter of "excess and deficiency." This article reviews the context-dependent roles of iron, copper, zinc, aluminum, and manganese in the pathogenesis of AD, with a particular focus on their bidirectional interactions with classic AD pathology (the ferroptosis hypothesis is relatively mature, while emerging hypotheses such as cuproptosis have not been fully elucidated). Metal homeostasis dysregulation can directly promote β-amyloid aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Conversely, these pathological processes can also alter the binding, storage, transport, and subcellular distribution of metal ions. Dysregulated metal ions function as "context-dependent" modulators of pathological processes. Their functional effects depend on metal species, concentration, binding state, subcellular compartment, and disease stage. Metal homeostasis dysregulation associated with AD may essentially reflect a redistribution between physiological and pathological pools. Ideal interventions should selectively neutralize pathological metal pools while preserving or restoring essential metal-dependent neuronal functions. By integrating the latest advances in the field of metal-targeted therapies (chelators, metabolic modulators, biomarkers, metal imaging, and gene editing), we emphasize that future treatments should shift from nonspecific metal clearance toward precise metal regulation and precision medicine.

abstract: Safflower is an Asteraceae oilseed crop valued for its high-quality unsaturated fatty acids (≈90% oleic and linoleic acids), natural floral pigments, and diverse bioactive compounds. These attributes underpin its applications in functional foods, nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals, and various industrial sectors. Safflower inherent tolerance to drought, heat, cold, and salinity positions it as a climate-resilient alternative to more temperature-sensitive oilseeds; however, omics-based research in this crop remains comparatively fragmented. This review consolidates recent advances across major omics domains. Genomics covers chromosome-scale assemblies, GWAS panels, QTL mapping, and diagnostic candidate genes for molecular breeding. Transcriptomics summarizes regulatory networks for flavonoid and oil biosynthesis, stress-responsive transcription factors (NAC, WRKY, bZIP, AP2/ERF), and seed developmental programs. The proteomics section addresses stress-inducible, therapeutic, and storage/lipid metabolic proteins linked to quality and stress adaptation. Metabolomics outlines quinochalcone and flavonoid pathway architecture, color-specific metabolic profiles, and emerging clinical and nutraceutical applications. Phenomics highlights UAV-based high-throughput phenotyping, RGB and multispectral imaging for salt and drought screening, and machine-learning-assisted germplasm authentication. Epigenomics focuses on DNA methylation and miRNA-mediated regulation. Finally, lipidomics and metagenomics consider oil authentication biomarkers, refining optimization, and microbiome-driven nutrient cycling shaping medicinally important compounds. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in multi-omics integration, CRISPR-based functional validation, genomic selection pipelines, and detailed characterization of root-shoot architecture under combined stresses. Addressing these gaps will advance mechanistic understanding of climate resilience and enable the development of stress-tolerant, high-yielding safflower cultivars with improved oil quality and bioactive profiles, thereby supporting climate-resilient production systems and high-value safflower-based products at scale.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined, and causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and calcific aortic valve stenosis. Elevated Lp(a) affects approximately 20% of the global population and is not meaningfully modified by lifestyle intervention or existing lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy. This review summarizes the biology of Lp(a) as a therapeutic target, evaluates the efficacy of currently available lipid-lowering agents against this target, and describes the mechanistic principles, clinical evidence, and unresolved questions associated with RNA-based and emerging small-molecule and gene-editing approaches to Lp(a) reduction.
RECENT FINDINGS: Four RNA-directed agents targeting hepatic apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)] synthesis have entered phase 2/3 development. This includes pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), and olpasiran, zerlasiran, and lepodisiran, which are N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). Phase 2 data demonstrate Lp(a) reductions ranging from 79% to approximately 97% on a placebo-adjusted basis, approaching the practical limit of apo(a) suppression, with favorable short-term safety profiles. A fifth, structurally distinct siRNA conjugated with GalNAc at both strand termini has recently completed first-in-human testing, sustaining reductions up to 97% through 48 weeks after a single dose without injection-site reactions. Recently, the topline results of phase 3 Lp(a) HORIZON (pelacarsen) were released and demonstrate a substantial Lp(a) reduction without meeting the trial's primary composite cardiovascular endpoint. Two further outcomes trials, OCEAN(a)-Outcomes (olpasiran) and ACCLAIM-Lp(a) (lepodisiran), remain ongoing. An oral small molecule, muvalaplin, achieved comparable reductions in phase 2 testing. Lastly, early non-human primate data, together with a completed phase 1 trial of an analogous CRISPR-Cas9 construct targeting a related hepatic lipid gene, support the feasibility of a CRISPR-Cas9-based gene-editing approach capable of durable apo(a) suppression from a single administration. The pharmacology of Lp(a) suppression is now well characterized across three distinct therapeutic modalities. Whether the magnitude of biochemical reduction observed translates into a meaningful and safe reduction in cardiovascular events across different populations remains undetermined and will be addressed by the ongoing outcomes trials.

title: RNA-Based Therapies for Lipoprotein(a) Reduction: Antisense Oligonucleotides, Small Interfering RNAs, and Emerging Platforms.

abstract: Herpes zoster (HZ), caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), remains a substantial public health burden, particularly in aging populations, due to the risk of severe complications like postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). While existing vaccines (eg. Shingrix®) have advanced prevention efficiencies, they present notable limitations, such as high reactogenicity and complex manufacturing. mRNA vaccines represent a transformative alternative with rapid manufacturing, precise antigen design, and favorable safety. This review synthesizes the current landscape of mRNA vaccine development for HZ, focusing on the rational design of antigen constructs, innovations in lipid nanoparticle delivery systems, insights from preclinical immunogenicity studies, and the progress of leading candidates into clinical trials. In summary, this review highlights the potential of mRNA vaccines to address the limitations of current options, potentially offering a new paradigm for safer, highly efficacious, and scalable HZ prevention. Continued clinical validation is crucial to realize this potential and alleviate the global disease burden.

abstract: The interaction with intracellular proteins shapes the pharmacology and toxicity of RNA drugs like gapmers and siRNAs. Here, we identify the RNA exosome as a modification-sensitive interaction partner of long, chemically stabilized, single-stranded RNA drugs. Using proximity biotinylation proteomics, we observe preferential binding of the catalytic exosome subunits DIS3 and EXOSC10 to oligonucleotides stabilized by 2'-ribose modifications and phosphorothioate linkages. RNA drug binding correlates with exosome impairment as measured by dose-dependent stabilization of promoter upstream transcripts and accumulation of ribosomal RNA processing intermediates leading to reduced cell viability. Consistent with structural requirements for substrate threading through the exosome channel, oligonucleotides longer than 24 nucleotides can impair exosome function. Systematic variation of ribose and backbone chemistry reveals that exosome inhibition is highly sensitive to the spatial arrangement of chemical modifications and can be mitigated by incorporation of bulky 2'-MOE residues or alternative internucleoside linkages like mesyl phosphoramidate. In contrast to the clinically established RNA drug modalities, class-specific liabilities of emerging ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides remain poorly understood. Importantly, we demonstrate that ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides can be designed that preserve editing activity while minimizing exosome interference. These findings illuminate critical variables that must be considered in the safer design of next-generation RNA base editing therapeutics.
